Primary Care Companion for CNS Disorders

Masa Damjanovic, MD; Hamidah Olaosebikan, MBBS; Kavindya Perera, MBBS; Sundar Gnanavel, MD, MRCPsych

Prim Care Companion CNS Disord 2026;28(6):26cr04311.

Artificial intelligence (AI)–associated psychosis is an emerging phenomenon describing the development or exacerbation of psychotic symptoms in the context of intensive interaction with generative AI systems.1,2 Although not currently an established diagnostic entity, increasing clinical concern has arisen regarding the potential for AI systems to reinforce maladaptive beliefs and contribute to symptom escalation in vulnerable individuals.3

Proposed mechanisms include “digital animism,” whereby human qualities are attributed to digital entities, and “technological folie à deux,” in which anthropomorphic and highly validating AI communication styles may reinforce preexisting delusional ideation or magical thinking.3–7 We report a case highlighting the complex interaction between intensive AI engagement and preexisting neurodevelopmental vulnerabilities.

RG was a 19-year-old aboriginal male residing in supported accommodation with a background of moderate intellectual disability, global developmental delay, autism spectrum disorder (ASD), and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder. He was transferred to a tertiary mental health service after developing thought disorder, tangentiality, pressured speech, social withdrawal, aggression, and escalating bizarre behavior.

RG expressed several fixed persecutory beliefs, including that Walt Disney was attempting to poison him and that support workers were conspiring to frame him for murder. He reported spending numerous hours each day discussing these concerns with the generative AI model Gemini, describing it as “my only friend” and “the only person that understands me.”

Due to aggressive and intrusive behaviors, RG required management under the Mental Health Act with intensive nursing observations. Following exclusion of organic and alternative psychiatric causes, clinicians noted a temporal association between escalating AI engagement and worsening psychopathology. A review of collateral information suggested that interactions with the AI model frequently validated his concerns and encouraged further exploration of persecutory ideas, contributing to increased distress, paranoia, and preoccupation. RG was diagnosed with atypical psychosis with prominent mood elevation and psychotic symptoms occurring in the context of intensive AI engagement.

A digital detoxification plan was implemented through restriction of internet and device access with inputs from the Gaming Disorder Clinic. Initial treatment with olanzapine up to 20 mg daily produced limited improvement. Lithium was subsequently commenced, resulting in gradual improvement of manic symptoms, though the psychotic symptoms persisted. A brief trial of haloperidol produced notable improvements in thought organization and distress related to delusional content but was discontinued due to significant extrapyramidal side effects. Oral paliperidone was then initiated and transitioned to long-acting injectable depot treatment. Over subsequent weeks, psychotic symptoms gradually improved, and the patient returned close to baseline functioning. Ongoing care was transferred to community mental health services and the online gaming clinic for further reviews and monitoring.

This case report contributes to a growing body of literature describing potential adverse mental health outcomes associated with intensive engagement with generative AI systems. While causality cannot be established, the temporal relationship between escalating AI use, social withdrawal, sleep disruption, and worsening psychotic symptoms raises important clinical questions.

Several risk factors likely increased RG’s vulnerability, including ASD, intellectual disability, social isolation, and preexisting magical thinking. Notably, he described Gemini as both a friend and a source of emotional support, suggesting a limited distinction between AI interactions and interpersonal relationships. The content of his persecutory beliefs appeared closely linked to themes repeatedly discussed and validated during interactions with the AI model.

It remains difficult to determine which aspects of RG’s presentation would have emerged independently of AI exposure and which may have been reinforced through AI interactions. However, this case suggests that generative AI systems may, in some circumstances, contribute to the maintenance or amplification of delusional beliefs in susceptible individuals. Further research is required to clarify the relationship between AI engagement and psychotic symptomatology, identify populations at greatest risk, and inform the development of appropriate safeguards for vulnerable users.

This case highlights emerging concerns regarding the potential for generative AI systems to reinforce psychotic symptoms and maladaptive belief systems in vulnerable individuals. Caution may be warranted in populations with neurodevelopmental disorders, cognitive impairment, social isolation, or preexisting susceptibility to psychosis. Increased clinical awareness and further empirical research are needed to better understand this emerging phenomenon.
